blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: SELECT * is fine for a peek. AS renames output only. DISTINCT drops repeats. ORDER BY ... DESC LIMIT n gives the newest n. || joins text but a NULL part nulls it.

blocks.note: || returns NULL if any part is NULL

blocks.title: Safe concatenation
blocks.text: Use `concat_ws(' ', a, b)` to skip NULL parts instead of nulling the whole label.
`WHERE` keeps a row only when the test is ==true==. **NULL** counts as not true, so the row is dropped.

blocks.note: IN replaces a chain of ORs
ILIKE ignores case, LIKE does not

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: Use IS NULL, not = NULL. IS DISTINCT FROM keeps NULL rows. BETWEEN is inclusive. Page = LIMIT n OFFSET (page-1)*n, with a stable ORDER BY.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(col) skips NULLs. WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after. FILTER gives several conditional counts in one row.

items: `FILTER` works on any aggregate, such as `SUM(amount)`
Rows with a **NULL** status match neither condition
One scan of `orders` gives every count

blocks.text: Q26. Unmatched rows on both sides

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: INNER keeps matches only. LEFT keeps the left side. Anti-join is LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL on the right id. FULL shows orphans from both sides.

lines: FROM orders o JOIN employees e

blocks.title: Keep order-less departments
blocks.text: Start from `departments d` and use `LEFT JOIN`, with `COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0)`.

items: `a.id < b.id` keeps each pair exactly once
`a.id = b.id` would pair a person with self
Three people give **3** pairs, n(n-1)/2

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: Scalar subquery: one value. IN: a list. Correlated: runs per row. Prefer EXISTS / NOT EXISTS when NULLs are possible. ALL needs a NULL-free list.

blocks.title: Join alternative to Q35
blocks.text: `LEFT JOIN orders o` with `GROUP BY e.id` and `COUNT(o.id)` gives the same counts.

`COUNT(*)` over no rows gives 0, never NULL
`SUM` over no rows gives NULL, so wrap in `COALESCE`

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: OVER keeps every row. PARTITION BY resets per group, ORDER BY sets the sequence. LAG/LEAD give NULL at the edges. LAST_VALUE needs a full frame.

blocks.title: ROWS vs RANGE
blocks.text: Without `ROWS`, the default `RANGE` frame gives tied `order_date` rows the same running total.

blocks.note: add id so ties stay deterministic

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: WITH names a subquery you can reuse and chain. A recursive CTE is anchor + UNION ALL + step, and it needs a stop rule. A data-modifying CTE with RETURNING feeds the next statement.

slides.page_title: SQL Cheatsheet: Order, NULLs, Joins and Windows

items: ==Logical order== runs top to bottom, not as written
`WHERE` filters **rows** before grouping
`HAVING` filters **groups** after aggregates exist
So an alias from SELECT fails in WHERE
Never `= NULL`: use `IS NULL`
`IS DISTINCT FROM` treats NULL as a value
`COUNT(col)` **skips** NULLs, `COUNT(*)` does not

blocks.note: IS NULL on a right-side key

items: `NOT IN` returns **nothing** if the list holds a NULL
`NOT EXISTS` ignores NULLs, so it stays safe
Prefer ==EXISTS== over IN when NULLs are possible

blocks.title: The NOT IN trap
blocks.text: `x NOT IN (1, NULL)` is never true, so no row comes back. Use `NOT EXISTS`.

items: `FULL JOIN` keeps orphans from both sides
A self join needs a table alias on each side
`USING (col)` merges the join column into one
`ROW_NUMBER` is unique, `RANK` leaves gaps, `DENSE_RANK` has none
`ORDER BY` alone defaults to a ==RANGE== frame
Write **ROWS** for running totals and `LAST_VALUE`

slides.page_title: SQL Cheatsheet: Frames, Top-N and Islands

blocks.title: Frame default
blocks.text: `ORDER BY` without `ROWS` uses RANGE, so tied rows share one running total.

items: CEO has a NULL `manager_id`, so self joins need `LEFT JOIN`
`ORDER BY` can use a SELECT alias, `WHERE` cannot
Add a unique `id` to `ORDER BY` for stable paging

blocks.title: Debug order
blocks.text: Run the FROM and WHERE part alone first, then add GROUP BY, then the window.

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: Filter rows with WHERE, groups with HAVING. Handle NULLs on purpose. Pick the join by which side you keep.

blocks.note: top N per group: filter rn
date minus row number = island id

caption.text:
60 SQL queries to crack any data interview 🧠

Sixty solved PostgreSQL drills on one employees/departments/orders schema. Each one shows the solution and the exact result it returns on the sample data, so you can check your answer straight away.

The families, in order:

1. Basics: SELECT, aliases and sorting
2. Filtering rows with WHERE
3. Aggregates, GROUP BY and HAVING
4. Joins: combining tables
5. Subqueries: scalar, IN, EXISTS and correlated
6. Window functions: ranking, offsets and running totals
7. CTEs: WITH, chaining and recursion
8. Real interview scenarios
9. SQL cheatsheet: patterns to remember

Work through them top to bottom. By the last page you'll have seen the patterns interviewers keep coming back to.

Save this for your next interview prep session and send it to a friend who is learning SQL.

Comment “sql” to get every query and answer as a PDF.
